html:
Pergamon was a Greek city in western Anatolia, near the Aegean coast, and the capital of the Attalid kingdom from 281 to 133 BCE. It is shown here in 200 BCE, at the start of its greatest years.

Its founder, Philetaerus, was a treasurer who kept a large war chest of Lysimachus and used it to make himself master of the city. His heirs, the Attalid dynasty, took the title of king after Attalus I beat the Galatians, Celtic invaders, around 238 BCE. They sided with Rome against Macedon and the Seleucids, and after the Roman victory at Magnesia in 190 BCE, Eumenes II was given much of Anatolia.

The Attalids made Pergamon a showpiece. Eumenes II built the Great Altar, now in Berlin, and a library that rivalled the Library of Alexandria. Legend says that when Egypt cut off papyrus, Pergamon developed parchment, whose name comes from the city. In 133 BCE the last king, Attalus III, left his kingdom to the Roman Republic, which made it the province of Asia.
